sentences.text: Thus, the petitioner seeks, in present petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure that the FIR in respect of alleged offence under Sections 272, 273, 406 and 420 of Indian Penal Code and Sections 50 and 52 of Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 may be quashed.

1.2 The above quoted relief is prayed for in the background of fact that on 25.2.2012 the complainant i.e. Head Constable, Local Crime Branch Kheda reached along with the other police personnel the factory of the petitioner where they allegedly found oil packed in tins and bottles on which labels of different brands were pasted.

The complainant lifted three samples from each tin /
bottle and out of 39 bottles 13 bottles were directed to be kept at Police Station and other bottles were sent for analysis to FSL, Ahmedabad.
The complainant and team also seized other muddamal lying in the factory.
According to the complainant the seized material is found to be not fit for human consumption.
Thereafter, the complainant lodged the FIR / complaint which has been registered as C.R.-I No.130 of 2012 2.

Mr. Parikh, learned advocate for the petitioner has appeared and submitted that in present case the complaint has been filed against the petitioner with regard to the provisions under Indian Penal Code as well as the provisions under Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and the offences which are alleged against the petitioner are the offence punishable under the provisions of the both Acts i.e. Indian Penal Code (Sections 272, 273, 406, 420) as well as Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (Sections 51 and 52).

He also submitted that in view of the provision contained under the provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, police does not have any authority to initiate proceedings and it is only the competent and authorize officer under the Act who can initiate the proceedings by filing complaint before the competent Court of learned Magistrate.
He submitted that the proceedings initiated by the police are without jurisdiction and competence and therefore FIR filed against the petitioner deserves to be quashed.
3. So as to support his submission learned advocate for the petitioner relied on the decision in case between M/s. Pepsico India Holdings (Pvt.) Ltd vs. State of U.P. (2011 [2] Crimes 250).

entities.text: M/s. Pepsico India Holdings (Pvt.) Ltd vs. State of U.P. (2011 [2] Crimes 250)

He relied on the observations made in paragraph Nos. 26 to 28 which read thus:-
26.It
is not the case of the State Counsel that the carbonated drinks or juice based beverages are not intended for human consumption or that they are not substances for the purposes of section 3 (zw).
In PFA Act, standards were prescribed for various food articles in the Appendix B.
In Appendix-B, carbonated water is defined in Entry A.01.01.
By virtue of section 98, the rules including Appendix B has been temporarily transported to FSSA till the regulations under the FSSA are notified.
Therefore, we are unable to agree with the arguments advanced on behalf of the State that the provisions of the FSSA are not applicable in the instant case.

In view of the aforesaid crystal clear legal proposition and particular provisions under the FSSA we are in agreement with the arguments advanced by the petitioner's Counsel that for adulteration of food or misbranding, after coming into force of the provisions of FSSA vide notification dated 29th July, 2010, the authorities can take action only under the FSSA as it postulates an over riding effects over all other food related law including the PFA Act.

In view of the specific provisions under the Babulal Khemchand Nanakvani vs State Of on 30 January, 2013 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/80736730/
4 FSSA, the offences relating to adulteration of food that are governed under the FSSA after July 29,
2010 are to be treated as per the procedures to be followed for drawing and analysis of samples as have been provided for.

entities.text: Babulal Khemchand Nanakvani vs State Of on 30 January, 2013 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The provisions of penalties and prosecution have also been provided therein.

Therefore, before launching any prosecution against an alleged offence of food adulteration,
it is necessary for the concerned authorities to follow the mandatory requirements as provided under Sections 41 and 42 of the FSSA and, therefore, the police have no authority or jurisdiction to investigate the matter under FSSA.
Section 42 empowers the Food Safety Officer for inspection of food business, drawing samples and sending them to Food Analyst for analysis.

The Designated Officer, after scrutiny of the report of Food Analyst shall decide as to whether the contravention is punishable with imprisonment or fine only and in the case of contravention punishable with imprisonment, he shall send his recommendations to the Commissioner of Food Safety for sanctioning prosecution.
Therefore invoking Sections 272 and 273 of the Indian Penal Code in the matter relating to adulteration of food pursuant to the impugned Government Order is wholly unjustified and no est.

furthermore, it appears that the impugned Government Order has bee issued without application of proper mind and examining the matter minutely and thus the State Government travelled beyond the jurisdiction.
28. In view of the aforesaid discussions, the writ petitions are allowed.
The impugned G.O. Dated 11.5.2010 issued by the State Government contained in Annexure-1 to the writ petition is hereby quashed.

Consequently, the FIR dated 11.8.2010 registered as case crime No.392 of 2010 under Sections 272/273 IPC, PS Cantt. District Varanasi, FIR dated 11.8.2010 in case Crime No.144 of 2010 registered as PS Rohaniya.
District Varanasi and the FIR registered as case Crime No.244 of 2010, PS Khuldabad, District Allahabad are also hereby quashed.
The concerned Magistrates shall immediately pass necessary orders for forthwith release of all the petitioners, who are in jail.

He also relied on the decision in case between Shambhu Dayal Agrawal vs. State of Gujarat (2003 [2] GLH 621).
4.

sentences.text: Learned APP has submitted that the police has conducted investigation and initiated proceedings and filed FIR.
Learned APP has relied on the provisions contained under Sections 154 and 156 of the Code and also Section 4(2) and Section 5 of the Code to substantiate his submission.

In this context it is appropriate to take into account the decision by this Court dated 3.9.2012 in group of petitions wherein the investigation as well as complaint / chargesheet and the subsequent proceedings initiated by the police authorities were challenged and the competence of the action as well as proceedings was considered by the Court.

In the said decision the Court framed below mentioned issues:-
1) Whether section 22 of the Act would debar even lodging an FIR before the police with respect to the offences punishable under the said Act and the Rules made thereunder ?
2) In case such FIRs are not debarred and the police are permitted to investigate, can the concerned Magistrate take cognizance of the offences on a police report ?

Babulal Khemchand Nanakvani vs State Of on 30 January, 2013 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/80736730/

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: What would be the effect on the offences punishable under the Indian Penal Code in view of the provisions contained in the Act ?

Thereafter the Court held that:-
21.

In the result, I find that :-
1) Section 22 of the Act does not prohibit registering an FIR by the police on information being given with respect to offences punishable under the said Act or the Rules made thereunder,
2) It is, however, not open for the Magistrate to take cognizance of the offence punishable under the Act or the Rules made thereunder on a mere chargesheet filed by the police.

It would, however, be open for the officer authorized by the State or the Central Government in this behalf to file a complaint in writing before the Magistrate relying upon the investigation carried out by the police and the compliant may also include the papers of police investigation.
3) With respect to offences punishable under the Indian Penal Code, no such bar as indicated in para (2) would apply.
In so far as the petitions where only FIRs have been registered by the police and no chargesheet is filed, they must fail.

In so far as the cases where police investigation has been concluded and chargesheets have been filed, it would not be open for the Magistrate concerned to take cognizance of offences only on such police reports.

5. In view of the facts of present case and in light of the decision on which learned Counsel for the petitioner has placed reliance i.e. the decision in case of Pepsico India Holdings (Pvt.) Ltd (supra)
and also in light of the decision by this Court in above referred group of petitions it appears that the petition requires further consideration.

Therefore below mentioned order is passed:-
Rule.

By way of ad-interim relief it is clarified that though investigation may be completed (if already not completed) and chargesheet may be filed (if already not filed) learned Magistrate may not proceed further i.e. may not take cognizance and may not initiate further proceedings until final hearing of present petition or until any other or further order is passed by the Court in present petition.
